Koschei's defining trait, shared with a wider international family of "externalized soul" folktales, is that his death is hidden far from his own body: commonly described as being at the tip of a needle, inside an egg, inside a duck, inside a hare, locked in an iron chest, buried under an oak on the island of Buyan. A hero (often Prince Ivan, in the best-known telling pursuing Vasilisa or Marya Morevna, whom Koschei has abducted) must work through this chain of containers to find and break the needle, which alone kills him. Koschei's abduction of a heroine and his vulnerability to a single hidden object make him a recurring foil in the same fairy-tale corpus as Baba Yaga, sometimes appearing in the same cycle of tales.

primarySources.text: Collected as part of the largest 19th-century corpus of East Slavic oral folklore.
primarySources.source: Alexander Afanasyev, Narodnye russkie skazki (Russian Fairy Tales), 1855–1863

name: Baba Yaga
description: An ambiguous witch-like figure of East Slavic fairy tales who lives in a hut on chicken legs deep in the forest, and who can be either a dangerous child-eating threat or a difficult but genuine helper who sets the hero a test.
habitat: A hut on chicken legs, deep in the forest, at the edge between the human world and the world of the dead
abilities: flight (by mortar and pestle, sweeping her trail with a broom)
commanding animals and elemental servants (dawn, day, and night, in some tellings)
detailedBio:
## A fairy-tale figure, not a pagan-era goddess

Baba Yaga is documented almost entirely in East Slavic fairy tales collected in the 19th century, above all by Afanasyev, whose collection preserves her best-known appearance in *Vasilisa the Beautiful*. No pagan-era chronicle or missionary account describes her; claims that she descends from a specific ancient goddess are modern speculation, not attested continuity, and this site does not present her as a pagan deity.

## An ambiguous figure, not a simple villain

What makes Baba Yaga distinctive within the fairy-tale corpus is her moral ambiguity: in some tales she is a straightforward threat who eats children who wander into her hut; in others, including *Vasilisa the Beautiful*, she is a difficult but ultimately fair gatekeeper who sets the protagonist an impossible-seeming household task and rewards honest, respectful effort. Her hut, famously set on chicken legs and able to turn to face the visitor, and her mode of travel — flying in a mortar, rowing with a pestle, sweeping away her tracks with a birch broom — are consistent across tellings and mark her as a liminal figure standing at the boundary between the everyday world and the world of the dead.

primarySources.text: Collected as part of the largest 19th-century corpus of East Slavic oral folklore.
primarySources.source: Alexander Afanasyev, Narodnye russkie skazki (Russian Fairy Tales), 1855–1863

name: Mmoatia
description: Small forest beings of Asante belief, often translated 'fairies' or 'little people', who live deep in the bush; in the tale of how Ananse bought the stories, a mmoatia is the last of the prizes he must bring Nyame.
detailedBio:
## The little folk of the forest

Rattray's Asante informants described mmoatia (singular aboatia) as very small forest beings, sometimes said to have feet pointing backwards, who could make themselves unseen, stole food and palm wine, and knew the medicinal uses of plants. They were said to teach that knowledge to some people, and Rattray recorded the belief that certain priests had learned their craft from them. They are not gods and are not served at shrines; they belong, with the sasabonsam, to the dangerous and unpredictable life of the deep forest.

## In the stories

In the tale Rattray printed as the origin of anansesem, the fourth prize Nyame demands for his stories is a mmoatia. Ananse carves a wooden doll, covers it with sticky gum, and sets it beside a bowl of mashed yam; the fairy eats the yam, grows angry when the doll does not answer her, strikes it, and sticks fast. The same sticky-figure trick travelled to the Americas and appears in African American and Caribbean tales.

primarySources.text: Describes the mmoatia as little forest folk of Asante belief who steal, can be invisible, and know the use of herbs, and associates them with the sasabonsam of the deep forest (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: R. S. Rattray, Religion and Art in Ashanti

primarySources.text: Ananse catches a mmoatia with a gum-covered doll beside a dish of yam, the last of the four prizes he brings Nyame for the stories (paraphrase).

name: Stone Giants
description: Giants of Seneca and wider Haudenosaunee tradition, shaped like people but of enormous size and covered with coats of flint that turned aside the arrows of men.
habitat: Mountains and caves of the Northeast
abilities: Flint armour that arrows cannot pierce
detailedBio:
## Coats of flint

Parker describes the Stone Giants, or Stone Coats (Gĕnnon'sgwā'), as beings like people but gigantic and covered with coats of flint. They are not gods: celestial powers such as the Thunderer can harm them, but the arrows of men cannot. The early Iroquois, he writes, were said to have fought many wars with them, and the last of them was killed in a cave. Several of the tales in his collection, including 'Beyond-the-Rapids and the Stone Giant' and 'The Stone Giant's Battle', turn on meeting one.

## An older record

The Tuscarora writer David Cusick's *Sketches of Ancient History of the Six Nations* (1827), one of the earliest Haudenosaunee-authored books, already describes 'stonish giants' who came from the west and troubled the people until the Holder of the Heavens destroyed most of them. The long record, from Cusick to Parker, shows the Stone Giants as one of the most widely told monster traditions of the Haudenosaunee.

primarySources.text: Parker describes the Stone Giants as gigantic beings covered with coats of flint, vulnerable to celestial powers but not to the arrows of men, with whom the early Iroquois fought wars (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Arthur C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales

primarySources.text: Cusick describes 'stonish giants' who invaded the country and were overthrown by the Holder of the Heavens (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: David Cusick, Sketches of Ancient History of the Six Nations

name: Horned Serpent
description: The great horned serpent of the deep waters in Seneca tradition, able to take the form of a handsome man to lure people away, and the chief enemy of the Thunderer.
detailedBio:
## Beneath the lake

Parker lists the Horned Snake (Gas'hais'dowänen) among the monster beasts of Seneca tradition: a serpent of the underwaters that can transform itself into a man. In tale 26 of his collection such a serpent appears as a graceful young man in fine clothing and lures a girl away to a lodge beneath a lake, full of trophies that turn out to be the skins of great serpents. When she realises what her husband is and flees, the serpent pursues her, and the Thunderer kills it with an arrow of lightning.

## The Thunderer's enemy

The hostility between the Thunderers and the horned serpents runs through Haudenosaunee and other Northeastern and Great Lakes traditions: the powers of the sky strike down the powers of the deep waters. Parker's tale ends with the Thunderer showing the people that the serpent's power can be contained, which ties the story to medicine practice; this site does not describe that practice.

primarySources.text: Parker lists the Horned Snake as a monster serpent of the underwaters capable of transforming itself into a man (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Arthur C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales

primarySources.text: A horned serpent disguised as a young man lures a girl beneath a lake; the Thunderer kills it as it pursues her (paraphrase).

name: Djogeon
description: The Little People of Seneca tradition, who live in caves and gulches, generally do not harm people, and, in return for small gifts, warn them of danger or help them to good fortune.
detailedBio:
## Little people of the gulches

Parker describes the Djogĕ'on as little people who live in caves, a people by themselves who live in houses as humans do and frequent deep gulches and the banks of streams. They can be tricky but in general do not injure people. They are poor hunters, and considerate people throw them small gifts over cliffs, including fingernail parings, which they use as hunting medicine, and tobacco when they are heard drumming. Out of gratitude they warn people of danger or help them to good fortune.

## Stories and continuity

Parker's tale 52, 'A Tale of the Djogeon or Pygmies', is one of several in his collection featuring them, and Little People appear in the traditions of many Northeastern nations. They are not presented as dangerous monsters so much as neighbours who expect respect, and stories about them continue to be told. This site does not describe any ceremonial observance connected with them.

primarySources.text: Parker describes the Djogeon as little people living in caves and gulches who rarely harm humans, accept small offerings, and warn people of danger in gratitude (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Arthur C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales

name: Nia'gwahe, the Monster Bear
description: The most feared of the magic beasts of Seneca tradition, a gigantic bear that challenges people to race for their lives and can be killed only by striking a hidden spot on the sole of its foot.
detailedBio:
## The racer

Parker names the Monster Bear, Niă'gwai'he'gōwā, as the most feared of the magic beasts and the one most often entangled in human lives. It loves to race: in various forms it tries to persuade people, boys especially, to bet their lives on a race that runs from sunrise to sunset. It has a vulnerable spot on the bottom of one foot, and unless a hero strikes that spot, it does not die.

## After death

Its bones, Parker adds, were prized in magic medicine, and dust from its leg bone was said to make a runner invincible, a detail this site notes without describing any practice. Tales 57 to 59 in Parker's collection, including 'Nia'gwahe the Mammoth Bear', tell of boys who outwit or defeat it, usually by finding the one place where it can be wounded.

primarySources.text: Parker describes the Monster Bear as the most feared magic beast, a racer that stakes men's lives and dies only when struck on a vulnerable spot on its foot (paraphrase).

primarySources.text: Boys outwit and defeat the Nia'gwahe in tales 57 to 59 (paraphrase).

name: Dagwanoenyent, the Storm Wind
description: The violent storm wind of Seneca tradition, which appears as a flying head with long streaming hair, set against the gentle wind Ga'ha'.
detailedBio:
## A head with streaming hair

Parker lists Dagwanoeient, the Storm Wind, among the nature beings of Seneca tradition and describes it appearing as a flying head with long streaming hair. It is the violent counterpart of Gä'ha', the kindly zephyr, and its passage tears through forests. The Flying Heads of Haudenosaunee story, enormous heads that fly through the air on their own hair, belong to the same family of images, and the Tuscarora writer David Cusick already described flying heads troubling the people in 1827.

## Kept apart from ceremony

Masks and the societies that use them are ceremonial matters the Haudenosaunee have asked outsiders not to depict or describe, and some winds and faces in Seneca tradition are connected with that practice. This entry is therefore limited to the storm wind as it appears in published descriptions and stories.

primarySources.text: Parker describes Dagwanoeient, the Storm Wind, as appearing as a flying head with long streaming hair (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Arthur C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales

primarySources.text: Cusick describes great flying heads that troubled the people in ancient times (paraphrase).

name: Kóoshdaa Káa
description: The Land Otter People of Tlingit belief, who take the drowned and the lost and slowly transform them into land otters, often appearing in the shape of a lost person's relatives.
habitat: Shorelines, islands, and forest edges of Southeast Alaska
detailedBio:
## The Land Otter People

Kóoshdaa Káa, 'land otter man', names the Land Otter People of Tlingit belief. People who drowned or were lost in the forest or at sea were said to be taken by them, and, unless rescued, to become land otters themselves. They could appear to a lost person in the shape of a relative or friend, leading them further away. Swanton's *Tlingit Myths and Texts* (1909) includes stories such as 'The Land-Otter Sister' and 'The Land-Otter Son', in which people are drawn into the land otters' world.

## Protection

Recorded accounts say that shamans could recover people taken by them, and land otters were closely associated with shamanic power. The belief is still widely known in Southeast Alaska, and stories about encounters continue to be told. This entry describes published stories and does not describe shamanic practice.

name: Gonakadet
description: A Tlingit sea being, the chief of a people under the ocean, whose appearance brings good fortune and wealth; often shown with the head of a wolf or bear and a finned body, and carved on house posts and mortuary poles.
abilities: Transforming a wearer of its skin
detailedBio:
## The wealth-bringer

Gonakadet (Gunakadeit) is one of the best-known sea beings of Tlingit tradition. Swanton's *Tlingit Myths and Texts* (1909) names Gonakadet as the head chief of a people under the ocean and records the belief that the sight of him brings good fortune, and he is associated with wealth throughout Tlingit art and story.

## The son-in-law story

A widely told story concerns a young man scorned by his wife's family as lazy. He secretly kills a sea monster, takes its skin, and wearing it hunts at night, leaving fish and seals on the beach during a famine. His mother-in-law claims the food comes through her own power, until the truth is revealed. The young man, now bound to the skin, goes into the sea, and in many tellings his wife follows him, the two becoming beings who bring good fortune to those who see them.

## On poles and house posts

Gonakadet appears on house posts and poles as a crest of particular clans. Edward Keithahn's *Monuments in Cedar* (1945) notes that the Gonakadet pole standing before Chief Shakes's house at Wrangell held the ashes of the father and mother of Chief Shakes VI; a duplicate now stands in the same spot.

name: Cihuateteo
description: The spirits of women who died in childbirth, honoured by the Mexica as warriors who accompanied the sun from noon to sunset, and feared because on certain days of the calendar they descended to crossroads to strike children with sickness.
habitat: The western sky, and crossroads on earth
abilities: Accompanying the sun to its setting
Causing paralysis and seizures in children
detailedBio:
## Women who died as warriors

Sahagún's Nahua informants, recorded in the *Florentine Codex*, compared a woman who died in her first childbirth to a warrior who died in battle: she had fought and been taken. Such women became cihuateteo, 'goddess women' (also cihuapipiltin, 'noblewomen'), and went to the western paradise, Cihuatlampa, 'the place of women'. Just as dead warriors escorted the sun from dawn to noon, the cihuateteo carried it from noon down to its setting. Book 6 describes the midwife's address to the dead mother, and Book 1 the cihuapipiltin.

## Feared at the crossroads

Their honour made them dangerous. On particular days in the ritual calendar they were believed to descend to earth and gather at crossroads, where they could strike children with paralysis or seizures, and parents kept children indoors on those days. Small shrines at crossroads received offerings to them. Young warriors, Sahagún adds, sought the hair or fingers of a woman who had died this way as talismans for battle, so her husband and kin guarded her burial.

## In stone

Several carved stone figures of cihuateteo, with clawed hands and skull faces, survive in museum collections from the Tenochtitlan area.

name: Maquizcoatl
description: The 'bracelet serpent' of Nahua lore, a snake with a head at each end, listed and drawn among the serpents of New Spain in the Florentine Codex; two-headed serpents were regarded as bearers of bad omens.
habitat: Fields and dry country of Central Mexico
detailedBio:
## A snake with two heads

Book 11 of the *Florentine Codex*, Sahagún's encyclopaedia of the natural world as described by his Nahua informants, includes a long chapter on serpents. Among them is the maquizcoatl, which the Nahua artist of Book 11 drew as a serpent with a head at each end. Its name joins maquiztli, a bracelet or precious bead, with coatl, serpent; the Spanish-era Nahuatl dictionary of Alonso de Molina glosses it simply as a two-headed snake, and the word could also be applied to a two-faced person or gossip.

## An omen

Like many creatures in Book 11, the maquizcoatl is described with its meanings as well as its appearance, and two-headed serpents were regarded as bearers of bad omens. The chapter mixes observation of real animals with lore about them, and it is not always possible to tell where one stops and the other begins; blunt-tailed snakes whose tails resemble heads may lie behind the image.

## Two-headed serpents in Mexica art

The best-known two-headed serpent of Mexica art is the turquoise-mosaic pectoral in the British Museum, which the museum connects with the maquizcoatl and its associations with omens and elite display; the object's precise meaning remains debated.

name: Nemean Lion
description: The lion of Nemea whose hide no weapon could pierce. Killing it was the first of Heracles' labours: when his arrows glanced off, he trapped it in its cave and strangled it, and its skin became his emblem.
habitat: The hills of Nemea, northeast Peloponnese
detailedBio:
## Hera's Nursling

Hesiod places the lion in the brood of monsters descended from Echidna: mated with the dog Orthus, the mother of the Sphinx (Hesiod's 'she' may be Echidna or the Chimera) bore the Nemean lion, which Hera reared and settled in the hills of Nemea as a plague to the people there. Apollodorus instead calls it the offspring of Typhon.

## The First Labour

In Apollodorus's account Eurystheus's first command was to bring back the lion's skin. The beast could not be wounded, so when Heracles' arrows failed he drove it into its cave, which had two mouths, blocked one entrance, went in by the other and choked it to death. He carried the carcass to Mycenae; Eurystheus was so frightened that he forbade Heracles to enter the city again and had him display his future trophies outside the gates. The lion skin, worn as a cloak with the head as a hood, became Heracles' constant attribute in art. Nemea later hosted the Nemean Games, one of the four great Panhellenic festivals.

name: Ladon
description: The serpent that guarded the golden apples in the garden of the Hesperides. Hesiod calls it the youngest child of Ceto and Phorcys; Apollodorus gives it a hundred heads; Apollonius of Rhodes names it Ladon and shows it lying dead the day after Heracles took the apples.
habitat: The garden of the Hesperides, at the western edge of the world
detailedBio:
## Guardian of the Apples

The golden apples were Earth's gift at the wedding of Zeus and Hera, planted in a garden beyond the ocean and tended by the Hesperides. Hesiod ends his list of the children of the sea-powers Ceto and Phorcys with a terrible serpent that guards the golden apples in the hidden places of the dark earth at its far bounds. Apollodorus makes the guardian an immortal dragon with a hundred heads, born of Typhon and Echidna, which spoke with many different voices.

## The Name and the Death

The name Ladon is best known from Apollonius of Rhodes. In the *Argonautica*, the Argonauts, parched in the Libyan desert, come upon the garden the day after Heracles has passed through: the serpent Ladon lies dead by the golden apple tree, shot with arrows dipped in the Hydra's poison, while the Hesperides lament. Apollodorus preserves two versions of how Heracles got the apples: by sending Atlas for them while he held the sky, or by killing the serpent and picking them himself.
